events.headline: New Liberal major projects bill clears first vote, heads to special committee | CBC News
events.evidence: A key piece of the Carney government's economic agenda, Bill C-39, passed its first vote in the House of Commons on Thursday, with Conservatives and the majority Liberals sending the bill for study by a special committee. The 243-page bill proposes to extend the government's approach to major infrastructure projects to other projects across the country. The government wants those projects to undergo one review instead of several reviews, and to have that single review completed within one year. The legislation is a core part of the Liberals' plans to pivot the economy away from reliance on the United States and present Canada as a reliable trading partner to overseas markets. Before the vote, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said his party would support sending the legislation to committee in order to propose amendments to what he called a "weak, watered-down, long-delayed" bill. Poilievre told reporters he wants the government to speed up the decision timeline on projects to between six months and a year, and to add measures to protect workers' rights. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says his party will be proposing amendments to Bill C-39. Prime Minister Mark Carney's government will use a special committee formed to study the sweeping legislation. Carney government to study new major projects bill with tool last used in Harper era Green Party Leader Elizabeth May said she also asked for committee standing but was denied. Critics warn Bill C-39 puts environment at risk At a news conference Thursday with labour and First Nations leaders, Davies and NDP Leader Avi Lewis said the legislation must not pass as written because of what it does to labour and treaty rights. Also on Thursday, Cold Lake First Nations filed in Federal Court for a judicial review of Ottawa's decision to designate the Pacific Link pipeline a project in the national interest. The First Nation accuses the government of failing to adequately consult with them on the project. "Last year I told the Senate that Bill C-5 was economic coercion. Ottawa used the threat of tariffs to push First Nations into line, and we got painted as the problem," Moore-Frappier said, referring to the Carney government's initial major projects law. events.headline: Ontario will officially begin removing Toronto bike lanes on Tuesday | CBC News
events.evidence: Ontario to begin removing Toronto bike lanes. Here's what you need to know Ontario will begin removing bike lanes from a stretch on Bloor Street W. in Etobicoke on Tuesday, the Ministry of Transportation says. A notice of construction start, issued by the ministry, says the work will occur on a 1.2-kilometre section between Clissold Road and Royal York Road. Dakota Brasier, spokesperson for Ontario Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria, confirmed in an email on Thursday that bike lane removal will begin Oct. "Following the ruling by the Ontario Court of Appeal, the province announced in September that it would immediately begin restoring motor vehicle lanes on Bloor Street West. That work begins Tuesday," Brasier said. T he Court of Appeal ruled in August that Premier Doug Ford’s government could rip out 19 kilometres of protected bike lanes in Toronto, reversing a lower-court decision made in July 2025. Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow said Thursday that the removal of the bike lanes is "completely unacceptable" and an affront to the city by Ontario Premier Doug Ford. "That is trampling on local democracy, the right of Torontonians through their municipal government to have a say over the municipal affairs of this city. Whether it is bike lanes, speed cameras, Island airport, every element we need to have our say. The city belong to all of us Torontonians through the municipal government," she said. The ministry-issued notice says existing pavement markings and pre-cast concrete curbs will be removed and new pavement markings and signs "to safely restore" an additional vehicle lane in each direction will be installed. Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow says of the bike lane removal: 'That is trampling on local democracy, the right of Torontonians through their municipal government to have a say over the municipal affairs of this city.' Michael Longfield, executive director of local cycling advocacy group CycleTO, said the organization is "outraged but not surprised" that the government has rejected the mayor's "win-win offer" to restore car lanes but keep bike lanes in Etobicoke. "Ripping out these protected bike lanes against the will of Toronto city council is a colossal waste of $48 million. The province’s own experts know it will not ease traffic congestion, it will put people’s lives at risk, and there is no network of side streets that could replace these lanes." The notice says crews will attempt to minimize disruption, saying access to businesses and properties "will be maintained throughout construction," as well as sidewalk access and emergency access. Ontario Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria said in a Sept. 1 news release that the government is committed to tackling traffic congestion.

events.headline: Syria Begins Destroying Chemical Weapons Remnants
events.evidence: Syria's Permanent Representative to the OPCW, Mohammad Katoub, announced that operations to destroy remnants of the Assad-era chemical program have begun, while warning that Israeli attacks hinder the process and that a timeframe for completion has not yet been set. Syria's Permanent Representative to the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW), Mohammad Katoub, stated that his country continues full cooperation with the organisation's Technical Secretariat to completely eliminate remnants of the chemical weapons program from the Assad era. He confirmed that destruction operations have already begun, describing this as tangible progress in the capabilities of Syria's national teams working on this sensitive file. The announcement falls within an internationally monitored process overseen by the OPCW, the body responsible for verifying the elimination of banned weapons programs. Ongoing work includes verification, inspection, and destruction of remaining materials and facilities linked to the former program. Katoub pointed out that Israeli attacks constitute a real obstacle to the removal of the chemical program's remnants, imposing security challenges and operational complications on field teams. In practical terms, these obstacles tie the pace of work to security conditions at the affected sites, making movement, equipment handling, and field coordination more difficult. events.headline: Bangladesh flood death toll rises to 44 as more than one million people affected
events.evidence: Relentless monsoon rains, flash floods and landslides have left at least 44 people dead and affected more than one million people across seven districts in Bangladesh, authorities said on Sunday, as emergency responders continued relief operations amid warnings of further flooding. According to the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief, more than 1.022 million people have been affected by the flooding, with 267,918 families remaining stranded by rising waters. At least 39 people have been injured since the severe weather began. The worst-hit districts include Khagrachhari, Rangamati, Bandarban, Cox's Bazar, Chattogram, Moulvibazar and Habiganj, where floodwaters have inundated 58 sub-districts (upazilas), damaging homes, roads, bridges and other critical infrastructure. Although rainfall eased over the past 24 hours in several parts of the country, flood risks remain elevated. The Flood Forecasting and Warning Centre (FFWC) warned that fresh short-term flooding could occur in Feni, Sylhet and northern districts, particularly along the Teesta River basin, due to continued upstream inflows and additional rainfall. The agency said water levels at seven monitoring stations on the Sangu, Matamuhuri, Kushiyara, Manu and Someswari rivers remained above danger levels, keeping low-lying communities at risk. Authorities have opened 1,131 emergency shelters, where 44,457 displaced people are currently staying after being evacuated from flood-affected areas. The Disaster Management Ministry said it had allocated 145 million taka ($1.2 million) and 2,650 metric tonnes of rice to the seven worst-hit districts to support relief efforts. Since July 7, district administrations across the country have also received 345 million taka and 6,900 metric tonnes of rice for emergency response operations. events.headline: US sets new demands for Iran deal: What are they?
events.evidence: US Vice President Vance’s call for reduced nuclear enrichment suggests room for compromise, but major obstacles remain. United States Vice President JD Vance has called for Iran to make a “meaningful” reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity as part of an agreement to end the war, a demand experts say may signal a softening of Washington’s earlier insistence that Tehran abandon enrichment altogether. His comments come amid hardline rhetoric from other senior US officials. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has reiterated that Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon, while President Donald Trump has warned the war will end through either “the nice way or the not-so-nice way”. Officials in Tehran, meanwhile, have questioned whether Washington genuinely wants negotiations as the US-Israel war on Iran enters its eighth month. As both sides stake out their positions, Simon Mabon, a professor of international relations at Lancaster University, told Al Jazeera that the prospect of Iran seeking a nuclear weapon has remained remote. Tehran’s negotiators are more concerned with sanctions, frozen Iranian assets, the US naval blockade and fighting across the region – issues he says remain the main obstacles to a deal. “If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60 percent enriched fuel?” The International Atomic Energy Agency reported that Iran had enriched uranium to 60 percent, below the roughly 90 percent considered weapons-grade. In its May 2025 assessment, it found no credible indications of a structured nuclear programme. Meanwhile, Rubio, speaking to reporters in Athens, accused Iran of missing several opportunities to reach an agreement. Analysts say the comments suggest pressure on Tehran remains central to Washington’s approach, even as Vance’s wording leaves open questions about what nuclear restrictions it would accept. events.headline: US unveils sanctions on ICC in move court condemns as 'assault on rule of law'
events.evidence: The Trump administration has unveiled sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) in a significant acceleration of its attempt to "dismantle" what it sees as a "rogue" institution. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the measures - which include a ban on US entities making transactions with the ICC - were intended to "defend US sovereignty" and accused the court of seeking to prosecute Americans. The ICC said the measures were an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order. The announcement came just hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The US has already sanctioned 17 of the ICC's judges and officials, but this move sanctions the court itself as an institution and is intended to collapse its ability to operate financially. However, the US has provided a six month grace period before some of these latest sanctions kick in, meaning member states can keep paying for its operations - a move Washington says is to allow countries time to negotiate a "solution to address" US concerns. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres called the US decision "a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar". They also praised the court's staff for their work bringing "those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice", as well as supporting victims. It is furious over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan the court has since closed and by its arrest warrants for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The Netherlands, which hosts the court in The Hague and is also a Nato ally of the US, faces particular pressure. Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has said the sanctions would seriously affect the court's ability to function. Netanyahu welcomed the sanctions, saying the ICC was "not a court" but a political body that threatened law-abiding democracies and "the very idea of national sovereignty". events.headline: China agrees to ‘halve’ hybrid car exports to EU in landmark deal
events.evidence: Brussels says Beijing’s shipments could fall by more than half over four years, cutting millions of vehicles amid fears for European jobs The EU said it has reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry. Trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič said the deal was the first of its kind and the result of “intense” negotiations with China since June to curb a trade deficit of €1.18bn (£1bn) a day, which has caused mounting tensions between the two economic powers. The deal “opens the prospect of cutting China’s export [of hybrids] by more than a half”, Šefčovič said, adding that this would translate into a reduction in exports of plug-in and battery-powered hybrid cars by “several millions” over the next four years, said Šefčovič said Šefčovič at a press conference in Beijing on Friday. “It is the first time that China has accepted to moderate its exports without going through the phase of prior trade tension,” he said, a reference to the usual investigations that must take place before safeguards under WTO trading rules are put in place. China has been flooding Europe with cars , including hybrids and pure battery electric vehicles (BEVs), threatening European manufacturers. Hybrids combine an internal combustion engine with a small battery. They are sold by carmakers as a transitional step towards BEVs. “This ‌is far from the end. It’s a crucial first step, but only a first step,” Šefčovič told ‌reporters in Beijing where he had travelled to hold ​talks with his Chinese counterpart. It added that both sides had “reaffirmed their commitment … to properly handle differences within the framework of WTO rules, and to continuing to stabilise and balance bilateral trade and economic relations”. While China and the EU acknowledged “differences” between them it appears that China has accepted the EU’s request to create a new model for trade balances starting with a pilot on hybrid cars.

events.headline: Hurricane Isaias downgraded after making landfall in Florida
events.evidence: Hurricane Isaias, the first of the 2026 Atlantic season, made landfall Friday night along the northern Gulf Coast of Florida, bringing with it heavy rains, powerful winds and the risk of life-threatening flash flooding and storm surges. Isaias is continuing north across the Southeastern United States after being downgrade from a hurricane to a post-tropical cyclone, the BBC's US partner CBS News reports . Florida, Alabama, and Georgia have each issued states of emergency amid warnings of life-threatening storm surge that could cause up to 9 feet (2.7m) of flooding in some areas. Isaias is one of three storm systems affecting North America this weekend, with the two others hitting Mexico and Southern California in the El-Niño fuelled warm waters of the Pacific Ocean. Both Florida and Alabama instituted mandatory evacuations to thousands of people due to the storm. In Florida, those evacuations include coastal communities in direct aim of the powerful storm. Florida Senator Rick Scott encouraged residents in designated areas to evacuate as soon as possible, as he warned in a social media post: "DO NOT WAIT! Get out NOW!" Hurricane Isaias is the first hurricane in the Atlantic's hurricane season, which largely has been delayed due to El Niño conditions in the Pacific. events.headline: Kenya's first Ebola case: Questions remain after man travelled across three nations undetected
events.evidence: Nearly 70 potential contacts have been placed under quarantine in Nairobi A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified. The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October. That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak. More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date. Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus. The account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell. The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there. His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care. Why Uganda is winning the battle against Ebola as virus spreads in DR Congo However, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town. Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease. events.headline: Putin tells Trump peace talks are unlikely, cites Ukraine drone attacks

Russian President Vladimir Putin has said an immediate resumption of peace talks with Ukraine is unlikely, citing drone attacks on Moscow during parliamentary elections last month. events.headline: US hosts ‘productive’ trilateral talks to end Russia-Ukraine war
events.evidence: US envoy Steve Witkoff says renewed negotiations aim to ensure lasting peace before winter approaches. United States, Ukrainian and European officials have met in Miami, Florida, to discuss a proposal for ⁠ending the Russia-Ukraine war, US envoy Steve Witkoff said in a statement posted to X. Witkoff said on Friday that “constructive discussions” tackled “potential avenues to de-escalate and conclude the war with Russia ahead of winter and advance efforts toward a durable and lasting peace”. Witkoff said the meeting included “the E3, the European Commission, Ukraine and NATO”. The discussions covered energy resilience, grain exports, security guarantees and “longer-term arrangements for Ukraine’s and Europe’s security to prevent future conflict”, Witkoff said. He also noted the “productive” talks discussed “Ukraine’s post-war reconstruction and economic prosperity, including EU accession”. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Thursday the conflict had reached a dangerous “stalemate” , with the failure to reach a negotiated settlement raising the risk of further escalation. The renewed diplomacy comes against a backdrop of deadly Russian attacks, including a strike on civilian buses in eastern Ukraine that killed 33 people. Hours after the deal, a Ukrainian drone hit a Russian fuel site. The Miami meeting follows visits to Moscow and Kyiv last month by Witkoff and Jared Kushner, as Washington seeks to revive negotiations that have yielded little progress.

events.headline: UNICEF Warns Impending El Niño Threatens Education, Health, and Safety for Millions
events.evidence: A mother and her child stand in the wreckage of their destroyed home in Toamasina, Madagascar, following a devastating cyclone. Credit: UNICEF/Tsiory Ny Aina Andriantsoarana UNITED NATIONS, Oct 9 2026 (IPS) - New figures from the United Nations Children’s Fund ( UNICEF ) project that the impending 2026-2027 El Niño cycle could be one of the strongest on record. Marked by unusually wet and dry conditions, this cycle is forecast to trigger a host of extreme weather events, threatening the health, security, education, and development of over 347 million children worldwide. “For children, El Niño is far more than a weather pattern. It can mean increased displacement, malnutrition, water shortages, and disease outbreaks. Children are also at risk of schools closing, while families could experience added financial hardship,” said UNICEF Executive Director Catherine Russell, emphasizing that anticipatory action is critical in protecting communities from climate shocks in the coming months. Nearly half of the world’s children—roughly 1.1 billion—are already exposed to at least three overlapping climate hazards, including droughts, extreme heat, and floods. The impending El Niño cycle could affect children and communities across nearly 100 countries and territories between October and December 2026. Rohini Sampoornam Swaminathan, UNICEF Statistics and Monitoring Manager, tells IPS that children are uniquely vulnerable because of their early developmental stage and dependence on essential services and caregivers. The Asia-Pacific region is projected to face the heaviest toll, with roughly 190 million children estimated to be at risk. Substantial populations are also critically vulnerable across East and Southern Africa, with 41 million children vulnerable to climate shocks, alongside another 41 million in Latin America and the Caribbean. Approximately 22 million children are similarly vulnerable in Europe and Central Asia, followed by 20 million in the Middle East and North Africa, and 20 million in West and Central Africa. Between 2016 and 2023, weather-related disasters displaced more than 20,000 children daily. In 2025 alone, extreme weather patterns interrupted education for an estimated 171 million students globally. “Despite efforts to plan for disasters, most resources are mobilized only after the damage occurs, and the focus is often on the immediate response phase of a crisis,” said Swaminathan. “With forecasts providing months of warning, UNICEF is urging governments, donors, and partners to act before needs escalate by investing early and before impacts peak. Building resilience is not only about infrastructure and early warning systems, but also about strengthening the services and institutions children rely on and addressing the inequalities that make some communities far more vulnerable to climate shocks than others.”

events.headline: Major quake hits Panama, no deaths reported
events.evidence: A powerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake rocked Panama on Friday, collapsing buildings and roads in the center of the country and injuring at least two people, with no deaths reported. The shallow tremor was felt across the Central American nation of around 4.5 million people, according to the National Civil Protection System. The head of emergency operations Rene Garcia told AFP that so far there were no reports of fatalities. In Panama City, about 200 kilometers (120 miles) from the epicenter, there were scenes of panic as people rushed to evacuate from the city's emblematic skyscrapers. "I was scared because the shaking was very strong and prolonged," Salomon Andion, 46, told AFP after evacuating his 15-story building for the second time following aftershocks. "Heavy objects like dressers, the bed, and all the kitchen items were shaking." A video widely shared on social media showed water falling from the rooftop pool of a building more than 20 stories tall. Carney’s top target has been a new oil pipeline to the west coast, which was designated a project of national interest last week, effectively deeming it pre-approved, subject to a number of conditions. Business leaders, at first skeptical of Carney’s pledge to make Canada an energy superpower and loosen Justin Trudeau ’s regulations that stifled resource development, are increasingly getting on board and praising the prime minister’s pro-investment policies. In a span of less than two weeks, Carney held the country’s first investment summit, announced a major new tax break for capital spending, and introduced legislation to reform the project approval process and make it easier to end labour strikes. A poll by Abacus Data and Vantage found two-thirds of Canadians want major projects built faster, but appetite is weaker for shortening environmental reviews or approving projects without Indigenous support. events.headline: Iraq expects to start transporting crude oil by lorry to Syria from mid-October | The National
events.evidence: Iraq is expecting to begin transporting crude oil via a route to be provided by Syria starting in mid-October, a development that is expected to boost its energy exports that have been hampered by flare-ups in the Strait of Hormuz amid the war in Iran . The crude products will be moved to a port in the Mediterranean Sea using lorries after Iraq requested assistance from Syrian authorities , Bloomberg reported on Friday, citing Yousef Qiblawy, chief executive of the state-owned Syrian Petroleum. The agreement between Baghdad and Damascus is “almost done”, and the Iraqi oil exports are expected to “start as soon as possible ... hopefully, by mid-October the first chain of trucks with crude will come to Syria”, he said. The impending move follows a similar energy trade-related co-ordination between the two Middle East nations in late September, in which Iraq began importing petrol through Syria . In April, Syria became the main route for Iraqi fuel oil exports, partially compensating for the disruption to shipments caused by the war in Iran. At least 2.1 million tonnes of Iraqi fuel oil have also flowed by lorry to Syria's Baniyas since then. An Iraqi Oil Ministry official had told The National that the first cargo of imported petrol, comprising 32,000 tonnes, was being unloaded at the Baniyas refinery, to be transported to Iraq on lorries. Opec's second-largest producer depends on oil for at least 90 per cent of its revenue. Most of its exports – about 3.3 million barrels a day before the war – crossed the Strait of Hormuz after leaving its southern Basra terminals. The seven-day moving average for crude exports from the Gulf was 18.3 million barrels per day on September 30, compared to the average 18 million bpd that passed through the region in the 12 months before the Iran war began, according to the ship-tracking firm Kpler. Last Sunday, the state-owned Iraqi Oil Tankers Company transported two million barrels of its own crude beyond the Strait of Hormuz for the first time in decades. The move was intended to shift part of Iraq's oil exports from the existing free-on-board Basra port model to transit the strait and take advantage of better sale and pricing opportunities, director general Ali Qais said, adding that the company is also in talks to buy specialised crude tankers “as soon as possible and to compete with regional peers”.

events.headline: Rooppur Unit 1 gets nod to start first controlled nuclear reaction
events.evidence: Bangladesh has approved the start of a controlled nuclear reaction at Unit 1 of the Rooppur Nuclear Power Plant, clearing a key stage towards test power generation. The Bangladesh Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (BAERA) gave the approval today (8 October), allowing the plant to proceed to the physical start-up stage called "first criticality". Mahmudul Hasan, chairman of the BAERA, told TBS that the final "B-2" power authorisation for Unit 1 has been issued, allowing the project to move to the next stage. "There are further stages, C and D, after this," he explained. Mahmudul expects the B-2 stage to be completed within two to three months. Once the subsequent stages are completed, Unit 1 will start generating electricity, initially producing around 300MW, he said. Dr Md Zahedul Hassan, managing director of Nuclear Power Plant Company Bangladesh Ltd, said that in a nuclear power plant, heat generated through nuclear fission is used to turn water into high-pressure steam. The first criticality is a major milestone for Rooppur. At this stage, the reactor will be brought to an initial critical state at less than 1% of its rated thermal power, initiating the first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction. events.headline: Metrolinx Launches Woodbine GO Construction in Toronto - Railway News
events.evidence: Metrolinx launched Woodbine GO station works in Toronto to serve 7,000 daily riders by 2051, expanding the Kitchener rail line with new platforms and tracks. TORONTO, CANADA – Metrolinx initiated heavy construction on the new Woodbine GO station in Toronto’s Etobicoke North ward, advancing works on passenger platforms alongside planned utility and track installations. The transit hub on Highway 27 connects the Kitchener rail line, Union Pearson (UP) Express airport link, and local bus networks to accommodate up to 7,000 daily riders by 2051. Provincial authorities confirmed the project enables a fourth mainline track and resignalling program along the corridor, though total capital costs remain undisclosed. What Is the Full Scope of This Project? Woodbine GO station expands the Kitchener Line corridor by adding passenger platforms, integrated airport transit connectivity, and civil works for a future fourth mainline track. Civil contractors are currently erecting primary platform structures between the active Etobicoke North and Malton stations, with automated platform snow-melt loops and utility duct banks scheduled for installation in subsequent phases. Station projects integrating airport feeders and multi-tracking position commuter operators to capture a growing share of the global rail infrastructure market, which is projected to expand from USD 101.11 billion in 2025 to USD 126.54 billion by 2030 (Source: Mordor Intelligence, 2025).
